title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description:
Given a string `s`, return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.

If several palindromic substrings share the maximum length, any one of them is accepted.
constraints: s consists of digits and English letters.
hints: Checking every substring is O(n^3). Think about where a palindrome is centred instead.
There are 2n - 1 centres (each character, and each gap between characters). Expand outwards from each centre while the ends match.
Track the best (start, length). The DP table dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and dp[i+1][j-1] is an alternative O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space approach.
approach:
**Every palindrome has a centre, and there are only `2n - 1` of them.** For each index treat it as the middle of an odd palindrome and the gap after it as the middle of an even one, then expand two pointers outward while `s[lo] == s[hi]`. The widest expansion over all centres is the answer.

**Why it works:** a palindrome of length L centred at c contains the palindromes of length L-2, L-4, ... at the same centre, so the expansion never needs to skip; stopping at the first mismatch is exact. Worst case (all one character) is O(n^2), typical inputs are much faster.

**The DP view** the interviewer may want you to name: `pal[i][j]` is true when `s[i] == s[j]` and `pal[i+1][j-1]` is true, filled by increasing length. It is also O(n^2) time but uses O(n^2) memory, so centre expansion is the better presentation. Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n) and is a reasonable thing to mention without being asked to code.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting the even-length centres (fails on "cbbd"), off-by-one when converting the final (lo, hi) back to a slice (`lo + 1` to `hi - 1` inclusive), and the brute force O(n^3) check.

**Interview follow-ups:** Count all palindromic substrings instead (same loop, count each successful expansion). Longest palindromic *subsequence* (2-D DP on s and reversed s). Can you do O(n)? (Manacher.)
